title: Functions
description: Defining and calling functions: parameters, arguments, *args/**kwargs, return, docstrings, and scope.
objectives: Define functions with positional, keyword, and default parameters
Understand return values, including multiple returns via tuples
Understand local/global/nonlocal scope and first-class functions

content.heading: Defining and Calling Functions
content.body:
Functions are defined with def name(parameters):, and called with name(arguments). Parameters can have default values (def greet(name="World"):), making them optional at the call site. Arguments can be passed positionally (matched by order) or by keyword (matched by name, e.g. greet(name="Asha")), and keyword arguments can appear in any order as long as they come after positional ones. A docstring — a string literal as the very first statement in a function body — documents what the function does and is accessible via help(func) or func.__doc__.

Variable-length arguments let a function accept an arbitrary number of inputs: *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple, and **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dict. These are commonly used for wrapper/decorator functions that need to forward arbitrary arguments to another function.

content.heading: Return Values and Scope
content.body:
return sends a value back to the caller and immediately exits the function; a function with no return statement (or a bare return) implicitly returns None. To 'return multiple values', a function actually returns a single tuple, which the caller typically unpacks: return min_val, max_val, then lo, hi = find_range(numbers).

Every function has its own local scope for variables assigned inside it. Reading a name that isn't local falls back to the enclosing (nonlocal), then global (module-level), then built-in scope — this lookup order is called LEGB. Assigning to a name inside a function makes it local by default, even if a same-named global exists; to instead modify a global from inside a function, you must declare it explicitly with the global keyword (or nonlocal, for enclosing-function variables in nested functions). Functions are first-class objects in Python: they can be assigned to variables, stored in data structures, and passed as arguments to other functions.

content.explanation: *hobbies collects any extra positional arguments as a tuple; **extra collects any extra keyword arguments as a dict. min_max returns a tuple that the caller unpacks into lo and hi.

keyPoints: Parameters can be positional, keyword, or given default values
*args gathers extra positional arguments into a tuple; **kwargs gathers extra keyword arguments into a dict
return with a comma-separated list actually returns one tuple — 'multiple returns' means unpacking that tuple
LEGB (Local, Enclosing, Global, Built-in) governs name lookup; global/nonlocal are needed to rebind outer variables
commonMistakes: Assigning to a variable inside a function and expecting it to modify a same-named global without `global`
Forgetting that a function without a return statement returns None
Confusing *args (positional) with **kwargs (keyword) order and placement in a function signature
